note.note:
H&P – Super Detailed

Consult Summary:
32-year-old male plastic-surgery doctor with 1.5–2-month history of recurrent, transient right-sided sensorimotor episodes (paresthesia, limb weakness, gait change, intermittent bulbar symptoms) now increasing in frequency, concerning for transient ischemic attacks; urgent referral to TIA clinic arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Weird symptoms” consisting of episodic pins-and-needles in right hand, subjective weakness of right arm and right leg, noticed abnormal gait, occasional throat sensation and difficulty holding coffee cup; associated fatigue and intermittent nausea.  
• Onset & course: Began ~6–8 weeks ago. Initial frequency once per week (patient vaguely also said “once a month”) → now several times per day. Each episode lasts approximately 3–4 days then fully resolves; asymptomatic at time of consult.  
• Progression: Increasing frequency; new mild bulbar difficulty (throat sensation, mild dysphagia) in last few days.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: None identified; spontaneous onset and resolution.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Fatigue, generalized weakness during episodes  
  – No persistent dysphasia, no visual disturbance; wears glasses.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives): No sustained headache, no chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, bowel/bladder disturbance, or seizures.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Screening blood tests after father’s surgery: normal cholesterol, blood pressure, and diabetes screen (dates not specified).  
• Asthma mentioned by clinician but patient did not confirm (conflict noted).  

Medications:
• Aspirin 75 mg daily – self-initiated; dose/route/frequency otherwise not documented.

Allergies:
• Penicillin (reaction not specified).

Social History:
• Occupation: Medical doctor (plastic surgery).  
• Living situation: Lives with wife.  
• Smoking: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol / recreational drugs: Not discussed.  
• No other lifestyle or financial concerns mentioned.

Family History:
• Father: Carotid endarterectomy performed for stroke prevention (history of carotid artery disease).  
• No other familial conditions noted.

Physical Examination:
(Remote video consult – no examination performed.)  
• Patient conversant, no speech deficit noted during call.  
• No vitals obtained.

Investigations:
• None to date.  
• Planned: Urgent TIA clinic assessment with carotid Doppler ultrasound and possible brain imaging (CT/MRI).

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Recurrent focal neurological episodes, ?Transient Ischemic Attacks (primary working diagnosis) vs demyelinating disease:  
• Assessment: Recurrent unilateral sensorimotor deficits with complete inter-episode recovery; strong family history of carotid disease. Episodes exceed classic TIA duration but vascular etiology must be excluded.  
• Plan:  
  – Urgent (within 24–48 h) referral to TIA clinic sent today.  
  – Expected tests: carotid Doppler, brain imaging, additional vascular and cardiac work-up per clinic protocol.  
  – Educated patient: If symptoms recur and persist or worsen, attend emergency department immediately.  
  – Provide clinic contact numbers (PALS and TIA service) in consultation notes so patient can confirm appointment.

Issue 2 – Aspirin self-medication:  
• Assessment: Patient taking daily aspirin without formal indication; potential bleeding risk.  
• Plan:  
  – Document current use for TIA clinic; decision to continue or discontinue to be determined after specialist review.  
  – Advise patient that dosing decisions will be revisited once etiology clarified.

Issue 3 – General health maintenance:  
• Assessment: No other chronic disease; allergy documented.  
• Plan: Routine preventive care to continue with primary care; ensure future communication of any new or changing symptoms.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Multiple Sclerosis, relapsing–remitting – Moderate likelihood. Age and relapse pattern lasting days with mixed sensory/motor signs; however, symptoms strictly right-sided and now multiple per day, which is atypical.  
2. Recurrent Transient Ischemic Attacks – Moderate likelihood. Unilateral episodes and family history support; duration >24 h argues against classic TIA, but vascular cause still plausible in young adult.  
3. Hemiplegic/complex migraine – Low likelihood. Can cause transient unilateral neuro deficits with nausea, but absence of headache and prolonged duration make this less likely.  
(Any additional DDx in system not discussed with patient.)

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Vital signs, detailed neurological and cardiovascular examinations, documented reaction to penicillin allergy, comprehensive medication reconciliation (dose/route for aspirin only), alcohol/drug history.  
● Conflicts noted: Clinician mentioned prior asthma history but patient did not confirm; episode duration (>24 h) conflicts with classic TIA definition yet clinician still favors TIA.  
● Transcript quality: Occasional connectivity issues but content intelligible; some timeline ambiguity regarding initial episode frequency.
